questions.question: In an orthorhombic crystal system axis angles, α = β = γ are
questions.answer:
**(A)** equal to 90°

In the orthorhombic system all three cell edges are of **unequal length** ($a\ne b\ne c$), but all three axial angles are **90°**:

$$\alpha=\beta=\gamma=90^\circ$$

(Compare: cubic — all edges equal and all angles 90°; tetragonal — two edges equal; rhombohedral — all edges equal and all angles equal but not 90°; monoclinic — one angle not 90°; triclinic — no angle 90°.)

questions.question: An example of trimolecular reaction is
questions.answer:
**(C)** $\ce{2NO + Br2 -> 2NOBr}$

A **trimolecular** (third-order elementary) reaction involves the simultaneous collision of three species — here two NO molecules and one Br$_2$:

$$\ce{2NO + Br2 -> 2NOBr}$$

$$\text{rate}=k[\ce{NO}]^2[\ce{Br2}]$$

The options in (a) and (b) are unimolecular and bimolecular respectively. True termolecular steps are rare, because a simultaneous three-body collision is improbable — most 'third-order' reactions are in fact complex.

questions.question: The reaction of benzene with an alkyl halide in the presence of anhydrous AlCl$_3$ is
questions.answer:
**(A)** Friedel-Crafts reaction

An alkyl halide with anhydrous AlCl$_3$ generates a carbocation, which attacks the ring:

$$\ce{C6H6 + CH3Cl ->[AlCl3] C6H5CH3 + HCl}$$

This electrophilic substitution is the **Friedel-Crafts alkylation**. (The Gattermann-Koch reaction formylates benzene with CO + HCl over AlCl$_3$/CuCl; the Rosenmund reduction converts an acid chloride to an aldehyde. *The reaction equation itself is missing from the printed scan — only its options survive — so the stem above restates it from the keyed answer.*)

questions.question: Malachite is an ore of
questions.answer:
**(B)** Cu

**Malachite** is basic copper(II) carbonate, **$\ce{CuCO3\cdot Cu(OH)2}$** — a green ore of copper. It is calcined to the oxide and then reduced, or leached with dilute sulphuric acid and the copper obtained by electrolysis:

$$\ce{CuCO3\cdot Cu(OH)2 ->[\Delta] 2CuO + CO2 + H2O}$$

$$\ce{CuO + C -> Cu + CO}$$

(Other copper ores: copper pyrite CuFeS$_2$, cuprite Cu$_2$O, copper glance Cu$_2$S.)

questions.question: Ethyl bromide + KOH(aq) $\xrightarrow{\text{boil}}$ A; 'A' is
questions.answer:
**(A)** Ethyl alcohol

Aqueous KOH supplies hydroxide ions as **nucleophiles**, so substitution (S$_N$2) takes place:

$$\ce{C2H5Br + KOH(aq) ->[\text{boil}] C2H5OH + KBr}$$

The product is ethanol. Alcoholic KOH, by contrast, acts as a base and eliminates HBr to give ethene — the solvent is what controls which product forms.

questions.question: Propan-2-ol + [O] $\xrightarrow{\text{oxidation}}$ A; 'A' is
questions.answer:
**(A)** Acetone

Propan-2-ol is a **secondary** alcohol, and oxidation removes the hydrogen on the carbinol carbon to give a ketone — it cannot go on to an acid because there is no hydrogen left on that carbon:

$$\ce{CH3CH(OH)CH3 + [O] ->[K2Cr2O7/H2SO4] CH3COCH3 + H2O}$$

The product is **propanone (acetone)**. Primary alcohols would give an aldehyde and then an acid; tertiary alcohols resist oxidation.

questions.question: Glucose is an example of
questions.answer:
**(A)** Aldohexoses

Glucose, $\ce{C6H12O6}$, has **six carbons** ('hexose') and an **aldehyde** group at C-1 ('aldo'), so it is an **aldohexose**:

$$\ce{CH2OH-(CHOH)4-CHO}$$

Its ring form is a six-membered pyranose hemiacetal. (Ribose is an aldopentose; glyceraldehyde an aldotriose.)

questions.question: Benzaldehyde + [O] $\xrightarrow{\text{air}}$ A; 'A' is
questions.answer:
**(B)** Benzoic acid

Aldehydes are oxidised readily — even by the oxygen of the air — to the corresponding carboxylic acid:

$$\ce{2C6H5CHO + O2 -> 2C6H5COOH}$$

So benzaldehyde (oil of bitter almonds) gives **benzoic acid**, which is why it is stored in well-filled, dark bottles. *(Note on the printed key: it marks (c) benzyl alcohol, which is a **reduction** product, obtained with NaBH$_4$ or H$_2$/Pd, not with oxygen. Autoxidation of benzaldehyde to benzoic acid is the classic example used in this chapter.)*

questions.question: Calculate the rate of the reaction, A + 2B → 2C + D, given that the reaction is A + 2B → 2C + D.
questions.answer:
For the reaction

$$\ce{A + 2B -> 2C + D}$$

the rate is expressed with the stoichiometric coefficients as reciprocals:

$$\text{rate}=-\frac{d[\ce{A}]}{dt}=-\frac{1}{2}\frac{d[\ce{B}]}{dt}=+\frac{1}{2}\frac{d[\ce{C}]}{dt}=+\frac{d[\ce{D}]}{dt}$$

B is consumed twice as fast as A, and C is formed at the same rate as A is lost. *(The printed question gives no numerical concentrations — the data were lost in the scan — so the answer is the rate expression, which is what the paper asks for: 'rate of reaction = [A][B]$^2$' in the key, i.e. the order is $1+2=3$.)*

questions.question: Write the source of Vitamin A.
questions.answer:
**Vitamin A (retinol)** is obtained from **fish-liver oils (cod, halibut), liver, egg yolk, butter, milk and cheese**, and from the **$\beta$-carotene of carrots, green leafy vegetables and yellow fruits**, which the body converts to retinol.

It is a fat-soluble vitamin needed for the visual pigment rhodopsin (hence 'night blindness' on deficiency), for healthy epithelia and for growth. Being fat-soluble, it is stored in the liver and an excess is toxic.

questions.question: Write dispersed phase and dispersion medium of dust, a colloidal solution.
questions.answer:
In **dust** the **dispersed phase is a solid** (fine particles of earth, soot or pollen) and the **dispersion medium is a gas** (air).

So dust is a **solid-in-gas aerosol**, often called a solid aerosol. The same class includes smoke (solid particles in air) and fumes; mist and fog are liquid-in-gas aerosols. Dust is a colloid because the particles are 1–1000 nm and remain suspended by Brownian motion of the air molecules.

questions.question: Which polymer is prepared by the monomer, styrene?
questions.answer:
**Polystyrene** — made by the addition polymerisation of **styrene (phenylethene, $\ce{C6H5CH=CH2}$)**:

$$\ce{nC6H5CH=CH2 ->[-CH2-CH(C6H5)-]_n}$$

It is a hard, transparent, colourless thermoplastic, a good electrical insulator, used for disposable cups, packing, and as expanded foam. Copolymerised with butadiene it gives Buna-S rubber, and with acrylonitrile it gives SAN plastics.

questions.question: Write IUPAC name of CH$_3$C(Cl)(C$_2$H$_5$)CH$_2$CH$_3$.
questions.answer:
**3-chloro-3-methylpentane**

The longest chain through the substituted carbon contains five carbons (C-1, C-2 to the quaternary carbon, then the ethyl group supplying C-4 and C-5). Numbering from the nearer end gives the substituents the lowest locants, both at C-3:

$$\ce{CH3-CH2-C(Cl)(CH3)-CH2-CH3}$$

So the chain is pentane with a chloro and a methyl at C-3 — **3-chloro-3-methylpentane** (alphabetical order: chloro before methyl).

questions.question: What is the three-letter symbol of the amino acid, Proline?
questions.answer:
**Pro.**

Proline is the only standard amino acid whose side chain cyclises back onto its own nitrogen to form a five-membered **pyrrolidine ring**, so it is an *imino* acid rather than a true amine. Because the ring fixes the N–C$\alpha$ bond, proline introduces a kink in a polypeptide chain and is often found at turns in protein structures.

questions.question: Give an example of Tranquillizer.
questions.answer:
**Haldol (haloperidol)** — a butyrophenone tranquilliser/antipsychotic; other examples are **diazepam (Valium)**, **chlordiazepoxide (Librium)** and **meprobamate**.

Tranquillisers are central-nervous-system depressants used to treat anxiety, tension and (for the antipsychotics) thought disorders. Note that haloperidol is more strictly an **antipsychotic** — the milder anxiolytics are the benzodiazepines.

questions.question: What is salt bridge? Mention its functions.
questions.answer:
A **salt bridge** is an inverted U-tube (or a paper wick) containing a concentrated solution of an inert electrolyte such as **KCl or $\ce{KNO3}$**, often set in agar, which connects the two half-cells of a galvanic cell.

**Functions:**

1. It **completes the cell circuit**, connecting the two solutions so current can flow continuously without the solutions mixing.
2. It **maintains electrical neutrality** of the two half-cell solutions by allowing ions to migrate: as Zn$^{2+}$ builds up in the anode compartment and Cu$^{2+}$ is used up at the cathode, Cl$^-$ moves towards the anode and K$^+$ towards the cathode.
3. It **prevents the transference of electrolyte** from one half-cell to the other, and by using K$^+$ and Cl$^-$ (which have almost equal mobilities) it keeps the liquid-junction potential near zero.

questions.question: What is the role of silica in the metallurgy of copper?
questions.answer:
Silica acts as a **flux** — it removes the iron oxide impurity as a fusible **slag**.

Copper ores contain iron sulphide, which on roasting leaves iron(II) oxide. Silica is added before smelting so that it combines with the FeO:

$$\ce{FeO + SiO2 -> FeSiO3}\quad(\text{slag})$$

The iron silicate melts at the furnace temperature, is much less dense than molten copper matte, and floats on top, so it can be tapped off and the copper layer drawn from below. In this way the iron is removed and a reasonably pure copper matte ($\ce{Cu2S}$·FeS) is left for the converting step. *(The printed key calls the slag 'FeSiO$_3$', which is the standard simplification; strictly the slag is a fayalite-type silicate, $\ce{Fe2SiO4}$.)*

questions.question: What happens when — (a) Acetaldehyde is treated with hydrazine? (b) Ethyl iodide reacts with alcoholic KOH solution?
questions.answer:
**(a)** Hydrazine condenses with the carbonyl group, water being eliminated, to give **acetaldehyde hydrazone**:

$$\ce{CH3CHO + H2NNH2 -> CH3CH=N-NH2 + H2O}$$

The reaction is the ammonia-derivative version of imine formation and requires a slightly acidic medium; with phenylhydrazine the analogous product is a phenylhydrazone, which is used to identify carbonyl compounds by its sharp melting point. (Further heating of a hydrazone with KOH — the Wolff–Kishner reduction — gives the alkane.)

**(b)** Alcoholic KOH is a base, so **elimination** occurs:

$$\ce{CH3CH2I + KOH(alc) -> CH2=CH2 ^ + KI + H2O}$$

**Ethene** is evolved; in aqueous KOH the same halide would give ethanol by substitution.

questions.question: Give reasons for the following: (a) Transition metal and many of their compounds show magnetic behaviour. (b) The enthalpy of atomisation of transition metals is high.
questions.answer:
**(a) Magnetism.** Transition metals have **unpaired electrons in their $(n-1)d$ orbitals**. Each unpaired electron has a spin magnetic moment, and these moments give the atom or ion a net magnetic moment; a substance is **paramagnetic** and is attracted into a magnetic field. The magnetic moment obeys $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}$ B.M. and therefore **falls as the number of unpaired electrons falls** — which is why the paramagnetism of the $\ce{M^{2+}}$ ions decreases across the 3d series from Mn$^{2+}$ ($d^5$, $\mu=5.9$ B.M.) to Zn$^{2+}$ ($d^{10}$, diamagnetic). Where the moments align in domains (Fe, Co, Ni) the behaviour is ferromagnetic.

**(b) High enthalpy of atomisation.** Transition metals have **high effective nuclear charge and many valence electrons**, including the $d$ electrons that take part in metallic bonding. The result is very strong metallic bonds, so a large amount of energy is needed to break the lattice into gaseous atoms — the enthalpy of atomisation is high (e.g. about 400 kJ mol$^{-1}$ for W and Mo). This also explains their high melting points, hardness and low volatility.

questions.question: Complete the following: (a) $\ce{Xe(g) + PtF6(g) ->}$ (b) $\ce{XeF4(g) + 2H2 ->}$
questions.answer:
**(a)** Xenon reduces platinum hexafluoride — the first noble-gas compound ever made (Bartlett, 1962):

$$\ce{Xe + PtF6 -> Xe^+[PtF6]^-}$$

Xenon donates an electron to the extremely strong oxidant PtF$_6$, forming the salt **xenon hexafluoroplatinate(V)**, in which xenon is +1. The discovery showed that xenon is not wholly inert.

**(b)**

$$\ce{XeF4 + 2H2 -> Xe + 4HF}$$

Hydrogen reduces xenon tetrafluoride all the way back to the element, hydrogen fluoride being formed.

questions.question: What are nucleic acids? Mention their two important functions.
questions.answer:
**Nucleic acids** are naturally occurring biopolymers — long chains of **nucleotides**, each being a **nitrogenous base + a pentose sugar + a phosphate group**. On complete hydrolysis they yield phosphoric acid, a sugar (ribose or deoxyribose) and a mixture of purine and pyrimidine bases. There are two classes, **DNA** and **RNA**.

**Two important functions:**

1. **Storage and transmission of genetic information.** DNA carries the code for the sequence of amino acids in every protein, and it replicates semi-conservatively so that the information is passed to daughter cells and to the next generation.
2. **Protein synthesis.** RNA — mRNA as the working copy of a gene, tRNA as the adapter that reads the codon and carries the amino acid, and rRNA as part of the ribosome — carries out the decoding, so the genetic message is translated into protein.

questions.question: Write any two differences between thermoplastics and thermosetting polymers.
questions.answer:
| Thermoplastics | Thermosetting polymers |
|---|---|
| Can be softened by heating and **remoulded** repeatedly | Once set they **cannot be remoulded** — they char or decompose on heating |
| Low melting point; soft and flexible | High melting point; hard, rigid and brittle |
| Made by **addition** polymerisation, giving linear chains | Made by **condensation** polymerisation, giving cross-linked networks |
| Examples: polythene, PVC, polystyrene | Examples: bakelite, melamine, urea–formaldehyde |

*Any two contrasted pairs.*

questions.question: What is tincture of iodine? What is its use?
questions.answer:
**Tincture of iodine** is a solution of **2–3% iodine in a mixture of alcohol and water** (often with potassium iodide to increase the solubility of I$_2$).

It is used as an **antiseptic** — applied to wounds, cuts and the skin before surgery, it kills micro-organisms on the surface. It works because molecular iodine oxidises essential proteins of the microbial cell. It must not be used on mucous membranes or large areas, as iodine is corrosive and can be absorbed.

questions.question: Silver metal crystallises with a face centred cubic lattice. The length of the core of unit cell is found to be $4.077\times10^{-8}$ cm. Calculate the atomic radius and density of silver.
questions.answer:
**Atomic radius.** In an f.c.c. lattice the atoms touch along the face diagonal, so $4r=\sqrt2\,a$:

$$r=\frac{a}{2\sqrt2}=\frac{4.077\times10^{-8}}{2\times1.414}=1.44\times10^{-8}\ \text{cm}=144\ \text{pm}$$

**Density.** For f.c.c., $Z=4$ atoms per cell, and the atomic mass of Ag is 108:

$$V=a^3=(4.077\times10^{-8})^3=6.777\times10^{-23}\ \text{cm}^3$$

$$\rho=\frac{ZM}{N_A V}=\frac{4\times108}{6.023\times10^{23}\times6.777\times10^{-23}}=\frac{432}{40.82}=10.58\ \text{g cm}^{-3}$$

**Radius ≈ 1.44 Å ($1.44\times10^{-8}$ cm); density ≈ 10.58 g cm$^{-3}$** — which is the measured density of silver, confirming the f.c.c. assignment.

questions.question: A reaction is of second order with respect to a reactant. How is the rate of reaction affected if the concentration of the reactant is doubled?
questions.answer:
For a reaction second order in A:

$$\text{rate}=k[\ce{A}]^2$$

If the concentration is doubled, $[\ce{A}]'=2[\ce{A}]$:

$$\text{rate}'=k(2[\ce{A}])^2=4k[\ce{A}]^2=4\times\text{rate}$$

**The rate becomes four times the original rate.**

In general, doubling the concentration multiplies the rate by $2^n$ for order $n$: first order ×2, second order ×4, third order ×8, zero order unchanged. This strong dependence is why concentration control matters in industrial reactors.

questions.question: Explain the following terms: (a) Peptization (b) Electro-osmosis
questions.answer:
**(a) Peptization** is the process of **converting a precipitate into a colloidal sol** by shaking it with the dispersion medium in the presence of a small amount of a suitable electrolyte (the peptizing agent). The electrolyte is adsorbed on the precipitate particles and gives them all the same charge, so they repel one another and disperse instead of settling. Example: freshly precipitated ferric hydroxide is peptised by a little $\ce{FeCl3}$ (Fe$^{3+}$ adsorbed) to give a positively charged sol. Washing a precipitate with pure water, by contrast, removes the electrolyte and the particles coagulate.

**(b) Electro-osmosis** is the **movement of the dispersion medium (liquid) through a porous diaphragm or capillary under the influence of an applied electric field**, when the diaphragm carries a fixed charge on its surface. Because the liquid layer next to the charged surface carries the opposite charge, the field drags the liquid along. It is the counterpart of electrophoresis (movement of the *particles*): together they show that both phases of a colloid are charged, and electro-osmosis is important in the drying of soils, in clay filtration and in capillary flow.

questions.question: How will you bring about the following transformations? (a) Nitrobenzene to Aniline (b) Formaldehyde to Methyl alcohol (c) Propanone to Tri-iodomethane
questions.answer:
**(a) Nitrobenzene → aniline:** reduction of the nitro group, best with Sn/HCl (or Fe/HCl, or H$_2$/Pt), followed by liberation from the salt with alkali:

$$\ce{C6H5NO2 + 3Sn + 6HCl -> C6H5NH2 + 3SnCl2 + 2H2O}$$

$$\ce{C6H5NH3^+Cl^- + NaOH -> C6H5NH2 + NaCl + H2O}$$

**(b) Formaldehyde → methyl alcohol:** reduction of the aldehyde to a primary alcohol with NaBH$_4$, LiAlH$_4$ or H$_2$/Ni — or by the Cannizzaro reaction with concentrated alkali, where one molecule is oxidised to formate while another is reduced to methanol:

$$\ce{HCHO + H2 ->[Ni] CH3OH}$$

$$\ce{2HCHO + NaOH -> HCOONa + CH3OH}$$

**(c) Propanone → tri-iodomethane (iodoform):** the haloform reaction with iodine and alkali:

$$\ce{CH3COCH3 + 3I2 + 4NaOH -> CHI3 v + CH3COONa + 3NaI + 3H2O}$$

The yellow precipitate of iodoform is the test for a $\ce{CH3CO-}$ or $\ce{CH3CH(OH)-}$ group.

questions.question: Using IUPAC norms write the formulae for the following: (a) Tetrahydroxozincate(II) (b) Hexaamminecobalt(III) sulphate (c) Diamminedichloridoplatinum(II)
questions.answer:
**(a) Tetrahydroxozincate(II):** Zn(II) with four OH$^-$:

$$\ce{[Zn(OH)4]^{2-}}$$

Charge: $+2+4(-1)=-2$ (isolated as $\ce{K2[Zn(OH)4]}$).

**(b) Hexaamminecobalt(III) sulphate:** $[\ce{Co(NH3)6}]^{3+}$ balanced by $\ce{SO4^{2-}}$:

$$\ce{[Co(NH3)6]2(SO4)3}$$

**(c) Diamminedichloridoplatinum(II):** Pt(II) with two NH$_3$ and two Cl$^-$ — a neutral, square-planar complex:

$$\ce{[Pt(NH3)2Cl2]}$$

The *cis* isomer is the anticancer drug cisplatin; the *trans* isomer is inactive. *(The printed key writes 'Rt' instead of Pt for (c) — a misprint.)*

questions.question: Discuss standard hydrogen electrode.
questions.answer:
The **standard hydrogen electrode (SHE)** is the primary reference electrode against which all other electrode potentials are measured. It consists of a **platinum foil (platinised platinum) dipping into a 1 M aqueous solution of H$^+$ (strictly, unit activity)**, with **hydrogen gas at 1 bar bubbled over it at 298 K**. The half reaction is

$$\ce{2H^+(aq) + 2e^- <=> H2(g)}$$

By convention its standard electrode potential is taken as **exactly zero**:

$$E^\circ_{\ce{H^+/H2}}=0.00\ \text{V}$$

The potential of any other half-cell is then obtained by making a cell with the SHE and measuring the emf: a positive emf means the other electrode is the cathode and its $E^\circ$ is positive; a negative emf means it is the anode. It can be used as an anode or a cathode depending on the sign required, and its value of zero is the anchor of the whole electrochemical series. Its practical disadvantages are that it needs a supply of pure hydrogen, a platinised surface that is easily poisoned, and it cannot be used in solutions that attack platinum or react with H$_2$.

questions.question: Predict the product in the following: (a) $\ce{CH3OH + PCl5 ->}$ (b) $\ce{CH3-CH=CH2 ->[H2O/H+]}$ (c) phthalic acid $\xrightarrow{SOCl_2,\ \text{heat}}$
questions.answer:
**(a)** Nucleophilic substitution by chloride gives **chloromethane**:

$$\ce{CH3OH + PCl5 -> CH3Cl + POCl3 + HCl}$$

**(b)** Acid-catalysed hydration of propene follows Markovnikov's rule, so the OH goes to the middle carbon:

$$\ce{CH3-CH=CH2 + H2O ->[H^+] CH3-CH(OH)-CH3}$$

**Propan-2-ol** is formed.

**(c)** Both carboxyl groups of phthalic acid are converted to acid chlorides by thionyl chloride, giving **phthaloyl dichloride**:

$$\ce{C6H4(COOH)2 + 2SOCl2 -> C6H4(COCl)2 + 2SO2 + 2HCl}$$

*(The printed answer draws only one —COCl, i.e. the mono-acid chloride; with excess SOCl$_2$ and heat both are converted.)*

questions.question: Complete the following: (a) $\ce{Br2 + NaI ->}$ (b) $\ce{CaF2 + H2SO4 ->}$ (c) $\ce{NH4Cl(aq) + NaNO2(aq) ->}$
questions.answer:
**(a)** A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its salt — bromine displaces iodine:

$$\ce{Br2 + 2NaI -> 2NaBr + I2}$$

The liberated iodine colours the solution brown (or violet in CCl$_4$).

**(b)** A strong, non-volatile acid displaces a weaker, volatile one from its salt — the laboratory preparation of hydrogen fluoride:

$$\ce{CaF2 + H2SO4 -> CaSO4 + 2HF ^}$$

(HF attacks glass, so the reaction is done in lead or platinum vessels.)

**(c)** Nitrous acid (from acidified nitrite) diazotises the ammonium ion, which decomposes at once to nitrogen — the standard test for an ammonium salt:

$$\ce{NH4Cl + NaNO2 -> N2 ^ + NaCl + 2H2O}$$

Effervescence of nitrogen and a slightly acidic solution confirm NH$_4^+$.

questions.question: An antifreeze solution is prepared from 222.6 g of ethylene glycol, C$_2$H$_4$(OH)$_2$, and 200 g of water. Calculate the molality of the solution. If the density of the solution is 1.072 g mL$^{-1}$ then what shall be the molarity of the solution? / In a particular reduction process, the concentration of a solution that is initially 0.24 M is reduced to 0.12 M in 10 hours and 0.06 M in 20 hours. What is the rate constant of the reaction? [Given that, log 2 = 0.3010]
questions.answer:
**Part 1 — molality and molarity.**

Molar mass of ethylene glycol, $\ce{C2H6O2}=2(12)+6(1)+2(16)=62\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$:

$$n=\frac{222.6}{62}=3.59\ \text{mol}$$

$$\text{molality}=\frac{n}{\text{mass of solvent in kg}}=\frac{3.59}{0.200}=17.95\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}$$

Total mass of solution $=200+222.6=422.6$ g, so

$$V=\frac{422.6}{1.072}=394.2\ \text{mL}=0.3942\ \text{L}$$

$$\text{molarity}=\frac{3.59}{0.3942}=9.11\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

**Molality ≈ 17.95 m, molarity ≈ 9.11 M.**

**Part 2 — rate constant.** The concentration halves: 0.24 → 0.12 M in 10 h, and 0.12 → 0.06 M in a further 10 h. Since **the same concentration change takes the same time regardless of the starting concentration**, the half-life is constant at **10 h**, which proves the reaction is **first order**.

$$k=\frac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}=\frac{0.693}{10}=0.0693\ \text{h}^{-1}$$

Equivalently, $k=\dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{C_0}{C_t}=\dfrac{2.303}{10}\log\dfrac{0.24}{0.12}=\dfrac{2.303\times0.3010}{10}=0.0693\ \text{h}^{-1}$.

**k = 0.0693 h$^{-1}$**, first order.

questions.question: Give the principle involved in preparation of sulphur dioxide in the laboratory. How does SO$_2$ react with (i) NaOH and (ii) H$_2$O? / Draw the structures of the following compounds: (a) N$_2$O$_5$ (b) HClO$_4$ (c) XeF$_2$ (d) H$_2$S$_2$O$_7$ (e) H$_2$SO$_4$
questions.answer:
**Preparation of SO$_2$.** The principle is that **a strong, non-volatile acid displaces a weaker, volatile acid from its salt** — dilute sulphuric acid is added to a metallic sulphite or bisulphite:

$$\ce{Na2SO3 + H2SO4 -> Na2SO4 + H2O + SO2 ^}$$

Sulphur dioxide is a colourless, pungent, acidic gas, heavier than air, easily liquefied; it is collected by upward displacement of air.

**(i) With NaOH** — an acid anhydride dissolving in alkali to give the sulphite (and, with excess SO$_2$, the bisulphite):

$$\ce{SO2 + 2NaOH -> Na2SO3 + H2O}$$

$$\ce{Na2SO3 + H2O + SO2 -> 2NaHSO3}$$

**(ii) With water** — it dissolves to give sulphurous acid, a weak dibasic acid:

$$\ce{SO2 + H2O <=> H2SO3 <=> 2H^+ + SO3^{2-}}$$

This is why an aqueous solution of SO$_2$ turns blue litmus red and has reducing properties.

**Structures.**

**(a) $\ce{N2O5}$** — a planear molecule, $\ce{O2N-O-NO2}$: each nitrogen is bonded to two oxygens by double bonds and to the bridging oxygen by a single bond ($\ce{N-O-N}$ angle about 130°). In the solid it is the salt $\ce{[NO2]^+[NO3]^-}$.

**(b) $\ce{HClO4}$** — chlorine(VII) tetrahedral: three $\ce{Cl=O}$ double bonds and one $\ce{Cl-OH}$, i.e. $\ce{HO-ClO3}$. The extensive delocalisation over four oxygens makes it one of the strongest acids known.

**(c) $\ce{XeF2}$** — linear, $sp^3d$ hybridised, with three lone pairs in the equatorial positions of a trigonal bipyramid; Xe–F bonds are polar but the molecule is non-polar by symmetry.

**(d) $\ce{H2S2O7}$** (pyrosulphuric acid) — two SO$_4$ tetrahedra sharing a corner oxygen: $\ce{HO-SO2-O-SO2-OH}$.

**(e) $\ce{H2SO4}$** — sulphur(VI) tetrahedral about S: two $\ce{S=O}$ and two $\ce{S-OH}$, i.e. $\ce{HO-SO2-OH}$; the two ionisable protons make it dibasic.

questions.question: Write short notes on the following: (a) Clemmensen reduction (b) Wurtz reduction (c) Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction. / Identify 'X', 'Y' and 'Z': (a) $\ce{CH3COOH ->[NH3,\ \text{heat}] X' ->[Br2/KOH] Y'}$ (b) $\ce{CH3COCH3 ->[LiAlH4] X' ->[H2SO4,\ \text{conc.}] Y'}$ (c) bromobenzene $\xrightarrow{Mg/\text{dry ether}}$ Z'
questions.answer:
**(a) Clemmensen reduction.** Aldehydes and ketones are reduced to the corresponding alkanes by **zinc amalgam and concentrated hydrochloric acid**:

$$\ce{R-CO-R' ->[Zn(Hg)/HCl][\Delta] R-CH2-R'}$$

The carbonyl oxygen is removed entirely as water. It works in strongly acidic media, which makes it the complement of the Wolff–Kishner reduction (hydrazine and alkali) for acid-sensitive compounds.

**(b) Wurtz reaction (reduction).** Two molecules of an **alkyl halide** are coupled by **sodium in dry ether**, giving a symmetrical alkane with double the number of carbons:

$$\ce{2R-X + 2Na ->[\text{dry ether}] R-R + 2NaX}$$

This is a Wurtz *coupling*; the 'Wurtz reduction' is the same reagent system used to join two alkyl groups. It fails for tertiary halides (which eliminate instead) and gives mixtures with two different halides.

**(c) Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction.** A carboxylic acid having an $\alpha$-hydrogen is treated with **bromine and a catalytic amount of phosphorus (red P)**, giving the **$\alpha$-bromo acid**:

$$\ce{R-CH2COOH + Br2 ->[P] R-CH(Br)COOH + HBr}$$

The phosphorus converts some acid to the acid bromide, which enolises readily and is brominated at the $\alpha$ position. The product is a versatile intermediate for making $\alpha$-amino acids and $\alpha$-hydroxy acids.

**Identifications.**

**(a)** Acetic acid with ammonia on heating gives **acetamide**, which on Hofmann bromamide degradation gives **methylamine** (one carbon less):

$$\ce{CH3COOH ->[NH3][\Delta] CH3CONH2 (X') ->[Br2/KOH] CH3NH2 (Y')}$$

**(b)** Propanone is reduced by LiAlH$_4$ to **propan-2-ol**, which is dehydrated by concentrated sulphuric acid to **propene**:

$$\ce{CH3COCH3 ->[LiAlH4] CH3CH(OH)CH3 (X') ->[H2SO4, \Delta] CH3CH=CH2 (Y')}$$

**(c)** Bromobenzene with magnesium in dry ether gives **phenylmagnesium bromide**, a Grignard reagent:

$$\ce{C6H5Br + Mg ->[\text{dry ether}] C6H5MgBr (Z')}$$

Dry ether is essential: moisture would destroy the reagent by protonating it to benzene.
